div.p: This tool edits the detector response function (DRF) currently in use, or builds one from scratch when opened with a blank detector (the "Make without data..." button of the "Create Detector Response Function" tool, or when no detector is loaded). Nothing is changed until you press Use; Cancel discards the edits.

How the detector is modeled for sources close to the detector or off its axis. "Flat Disk" is the traditional model: the crystal is a disk of the stated diameter, and only the source distance matters. "Geometry Modeled" describes the crystal (shape, material, dimensions, dead layer, endcap layers) and uses that description to evaluate the response for any source position:

ul.li: No MC support (from measured curve): instant. The DRF's own measured efficiency (or its curve) is transferred to other positions through the ray-traced geometry. Accurate on axis and mildly off-axis; the reported uncertainty grows off-axis and very close in.

Quick MC and Full MC: run a Monte-Carlo characterization of the geometry (minutes), which is then corrected ("grounded") to the DRF's measured efficiency points when it has them. Full MC also models the response well off-axis and at contact.

div.p: While a response is attached it - not the curve or points on the Anchor tab - is what answers every efficiency and uncertainty question about this detector. So an edit the response does not reflect is an edit the program would ignore, and Use will not do that: it rebuilds the response (instantly, for No MC support) or offers to remove it and go back to the flat-disk model. Press Generate Response yourself at any time; whether a rebuild is needed is worked out from the content, so it is right after an undo or redo as well.
Fits, or lets you enter, the peak-width (FWHM) equation of the detector from the peaks in the current spectrum.

The efficiency this DRF states, and its uncertainty. Which editor you get follows how the DRF represents its efficiency - not the Flat Disk / Geometry Modeled choice, which is about where the detector can be asked about rather than how well it is known:

ul.li: A DRF from the "Create Detector Response Function" tool: the measured peaks, each with its absolute efficiency at its own source distance, its source, and its statistical and certificate uncertainties. The efficiency equation is re-fit from these points when you press Use, so the curve, its covariance and the points always describe the same detector. Editing a point therefore moves the curve; editing only an uncertainty changes how strongly that point pulls on the fit, which moves the curve very slightly and the uncertainty a lot.
An ANGLE .outx reference curve: the same table, where the points are the curve - absolute efficiencies at the one reference distance shown above the table.

A GADRAS Efficiency.csv or ISOCS .ecc curve: the curve's own energy/efficiency pairs, plus a per-energy uncertainty split into the part that is independent from one energy to the next and the part that moves together across energy (how strongly is set below the table).

An efficiency equation with no measured points: its coefficients and the covariance among them. For an equation that covariance is the uncertainty every analysis propagates, and fitted coefficients are strongly correlated, so the off-diagonal matters as much as the diagonal. If the DRF only ever stored per-coefficient uncertainties, the table opens on those with all correlations zero - a starting point that overstates the band, and one that is not written back unless you edit it.
An efficiency formula: the formula text, and either one flat uncertainty or a per-energy table of them.

div.p: Nothing you type is silently dropped or reinterpreted: if an edit cannot be applied - a cell that is not a number, too few points, a set of correlations that cannot describe any real errors - you are told why and nothing changes.

The line under the editor is what this detector actually reports at one representative energy, read through the same code the Activity/Shielding fit uses, and split into the part your data supports and the part that is a model envelope - an allowance for asking a model about a position nobody measured. A geometry-modeled response answers with its own budget rather than the curve's - which for a measured-curve transfer is that curve's uncertainty plus the envelope, and for a Monte-Carlo characterization is its own statistics and grounding fit plus the envelope. A detector with no measured uncertainty at all (a GADRAS Detector.dat) reports about 5% that is purely an assumed default plus that allowance. The band on the efficiency chart is drawn from the same numbers, with the inner band the data-derived part.

One thing to know before sharing: a DRF XML file (and an N42 with the DRF in it) keeps all of this. An app URL or QR code keeps the efficiency, the equation's coefficient covariance and the per-energy covariance, but not the Monte-Carlo response, the geometry or the raw measured points.
